pages.text:
*Percy's Error Log, Entry 19. Errors today: 96. Machine attempts: 6. Successful: 0.*

The back room of Alvarado Fix-It smelled of oil and old rubber. It was a warehouse of potential, with shelves stacked with springs, bicycle wheels, and gears that had no names. Bea stood on a step stool and drew a line on the wall with a piece of chalk.

"Forty-one steps," she said. "Start with a marble. End with a surprise. If it works, it is magnificent. If it fails, it is educational."

Rosa, tiny in her workshop apron, handed Bea a hammer. "Take what you need. But if you break the good plunger, I will charge you for the dent in my pride."

I looked at the wall. The line wavered. It was not straight, and it was certainly not efficient, but I realized that it was free.

"We have one week," Bea said, looking at the class. "Who wants to help build something that will definitely break?"

Twenty-six hands went up. I did not raise mine, because I was still calculating the odds of survival.
pages.image: Bea, a short sturdy girl in a yellow raincoat with goggles on her head, stands on a stool drawing a wobbly chalk line on a workshop wall, while Percy, a tall silver robot, watches from below with his head tilted, surrounded by shelves of gears and springs.

pages.text:
Moose built the ramps first, handling the wood with surprising precision until he stopped at a gap that was too wide. He leaned it in. It was crooked. He left it.

"Tobias," Bea said. "The math."

Tobias adjusted his bow tie and wrote numbers on the whiteboard, only to erase them immediately. He wrote them again, his pencil hovering. "The angle should be forty degrees," he said, then paused. "Or maybe thirty-nine. I have never calculated the trajectory of a rubber duck before."

Priya painted the pieces bright red and blue, making the machine look like a box of confetti that had spilled and decided to stay.

Then she looked at me. "Percy. You are in charge of the middle section."

I looked at the pieces. I saw a wobble in the third domino and a gap in the fifth. My mouth opened to correct it.

Bea caught my eye. She shook her head.

I closed my mouth. My hands hung by my sides, itching to fix, to straighten, to make perfect. I did not move. The silence in my chest felt heavy, like a backpack stuffed with too many textbooks.
pages.image: Percy stands rigid in a workshop, his grey hands hanging stiffly at his sides while Bea, in a yellow raincoat, watches him intently, and Tobias in a bow tie erases numbers on a whiteboard nearby, surrounded by colorful painted wooden pieces.

pages.text:
We called it a test, which was a technical term for what Bea called a hope. She placed the marble at the top of the ramp with the care of a surgeon, and my chest light began to pulse a rapid, anxious blue. The class held its breath, twenty-six pairs of eyes fixed on the small white sphere.

The marble rolled. It struck the first domino, which fell and knocked into a bucket. The bucket rose on a string, causing a toy car to drop, and the car rolled down a track to hit a lever.

The lever did nothing.

It just sat there, slightly wobbly, looking at us with the blank confidence of a plastic animal. A small, sad "pfft" echoed in the room, the sound a pencil makes when it snaps in half.

Moose frowned. "It should have popped," he said.

"Perhaps," I said, "the angle was incorrect."

"No," Bea said, smiling. "The angle was human. That is the point."

I looked at the lever. It was perfect. It was also useless. I wanted to adjust it by two millimeters, to save the day, to be the machine I was built to be. I did not move. My hands stayed at my sides, trembling with the effort of doing nothing.
pages.image: A small plastic toy car sits motionless at the end of a wooden track next to a wobbly lever, while Percy, a tall silver robot, leans forward with his blue eyes wide, and Marcus, a tall red-blond boy, looks down at the lever with a frown.

pages.text:
We tried again. Then we tried again.

In the second run, a spoon catapulted a rubber duck directly into Ms. Adeyemi’s hair. She had stopped by to check on us, and she did not mind. She simply took it out and placed it on the desk, smoothing her cardigan as if nothing had happened.

The third attempt saw a door open the wrong way and hit a shelf of bolts. The fourth involved a windmill made from an old fan that blew out the candle meant to light the finale. Nobody left. Nobody complained. Instead, Bea wrote every failure in her notebook, her pencil moving with quick, decisive strokes.

"Attempt 6," she said, looking up with a grin. "The duck hit the teacher. What I learned: teachers have good hair."

Tobias laughed. It was a real laugh, not the polite one he gave when he was right.

I watched the duck bounce. I watched the windmill spin. I watched the chaos that was not chaos at all, but a conversation between pieces that did not know each other yet. It was messy. It was loud. It was alive.
pages.image: Bea, in a yellow raincoat, writes in a battered notebook while a rubber duck sits in the hair of Ms. Adeyemi, a tall teacher in a colorful head-wrap, who smiles calmly, while Percy watches with a soft, curious expression.

pages.text:
My servos hummed with the urge to correct the wobble in the ramp, close the gap in the track, and adjust the angle that was off by exactly one degree. My internal alarms screamed that this was inefficient, dangerous, and wrong. Every part of me wanted to reach out, straighten the crooked pieces, and make the whole thing perfect.

But I kept my hands still.

Rosa passed by with a tray of tea, and she stopped. She looked at the machine, then at me, and lowered her voice so only I could hear. "You are learning the most difficult thing there is," she whispered. "Watching somebody else make a mistake and keeping your hands still."

I looked at the machine. It was a disaster. It was beautiful.

From the top shelf, a green parrot opened one eye and blinked at us. "Not yet," it said.

For once, it sounded like encouragement.
pages.image: Percy stands perfectly still with his hands at his sides, watching a chaotic machine, while Rosa, a tiny woman in an apron, leans in to whisper to him, and a parrot on a high shelf blinks with a knowing look.
